anchor: per window: language TTFT p99 < 1s and ITL p99 < 100ms; encoder delay p99 < 1s
claim_text: The evaluation SLA requires per window: language TTFT p99 < 1 second, ITL p99 < 100 ms, and encoder delay p99 < 1 second.

anchor: scored on provisioned GPU-time per hardware class (RTX 5090-class worker-seconds for the encoder pool, H100 GPU-hours for the language pool; never summed across classes)
claim_text: Policies are scored on provisioned GPU-time per hardware class: RTX 5090 worker-seconds for encoder pool, H100 GPU-hours for language pool, never summed across classes.

anchor: Language-pool GPU-hours bill from instance order, not readiness: the discrete-event mocker integrates the provisioned worker count --- active, starting-up and draining alike --- so the startup ramp and scale-down drain tail are already inside every reported language GPU-hour, and no cold-start surcharge may be added to it.
claim_text: Language pool GPU-hours bill from instance order (not readiness), including startup ramp and scale-down drain tail; no cold-start surcharge added.

anchor: Mixing the two conventions is a second reason, beyond hardware class, the classes are never summed
claim_text: The two hardware classes are never summed due to different billing conventions (order-time vs readiness).

anchor: Each policy produces, per window, a worker schedule for the encoder pool (C(t) workers) and a configuration or replica schedule for the language pool (TP×N H100 workers), graded on the two-pool replay.
claim_text: Each policy produces per-window worker schedule for encoder pool (C(t)) and language pool (TP×N H100 workers), graded on two-pool replay.

anchor: Scale-downs take effect immediately, guarded by a 3-minute hysteresis.
claim_text: Scale-downs take effect immediately with a 3-minute hysteresis guard.

anchor: under the stage-conditional metric the burst optima rise one to two workers but the deployable static C=8 is unchanged
claim_text: Under stage-conditional metric, burst optima increase by 1-2 workers, but deployable static C=8 remains unchanged.

anchor: First, every burst window forces the language pool to TP2, and the gain is the parallelism layout, not the GPU budget.
claim_text: Every burst window forces the language pool to use TP2; the gain comes from parallelism layout, not GPU budget.

anchor: At TP1 no replica count is feasible: the burst's ≈36k-token frames-class prefills pin TTFT p99 at ≈1285 ms even at N=16, a prefill floor replica scaling cannot buy down.
claim_text: At TP1, no replica count is feasible because the burst's ~36k-token frames-class prefills pin TTFT p99 at ~1285 ms even at N=16, a prefill floor that replica scaling cannot reduce.

anchor: Four TP1 replicas and one TP2×2 group are both four H100s, yet TP1×4 fails all five tabulated burst windows while TP2×2 passes each --- a 1.55--1.74× tail cut from layout alone
claim_text: TP1×4 (4 H100s) fails all five burst windows, while TP2×2 (4 H100s) passes each, giving a 1.55-1.74× tail latency reduction from layout alone.

anchor: intra-request tensor parallelism shortens the single long prefill that independent replicas can only queue.
claim_text: Intra-request tensor parallelism shortens the single long prefill that independent replicas can only queue.

anchor: Second, the encoder requirement swings from 2 workers on the calm day to 8 on burst5
claim_text: Encoder requirement varies from 2 workers on calm day to 8 workers on burst5.

anchor: Third, the single static fleet that survives all windows, C=8 encoders plus TP2×2 (4 H100s), hereafter the deployable static, overprovisions the calm day by 4× on the vision side and 2× on the language side.
claim_text: The deployable static fleet (C=8 encoders + TP2×2) overprovisions the calm day by 4× on vision side and 2× on language side.

anchor: It also carries a fleet-shape difference (TP2 versus TP1) that no replica autoscaler can morph at runtime.
claim_text: The fleet-shape difference (TP2 vs TP1) cannot be morphed by a replica autoscaler at runtime.

anchor: Close-out checks confirm the optima are robust to the router's tuning knobs (35 corner re-runs; no frontier movement).
claim_text: Close-out checks (35 corner re-runs) confirm optima are robust to router tuning knobs with no frontier movement.

anchor: Iso-cost tensor parallelism on the language pool: TP1×4 and TP2×2 both cost four H100s.
claim_text: TP1×4 and TP2×2 both cost four H100s (iso-cost).

anchor: The reactive baseline is Dynamo's SLA planner, the production controller of the platform this thesis targets
claim_text: The reactive baseline is Dynamo's SLA planner, the production controller of the target platform.

anchor: run through the same replay path in both its shipped load-based variant (A) and its SLA-target variant (B, ARIMA-driven throughput loop plus load loop).
claim_text: The reactive baseline has two variants: load-based (A) and SLA-target (B, ARIMA-driven throughput loop plus load loop).

anchor: Across the seven windows this yields 14 configurations, each at its window's optimal TP shape.
claim_text: Across seven windows, there are 14 configurations (2 variants × 7 windows), each at the window's optimal TP shape.

anchor: All fourteen configurations satisfy the planner's own control law (window-mean TTFT/ITL under its 500/50 ms targets) while violating the tail SLA (TTFT p99 up to 3,495 ms; burst windows additionally fail ITL p99).
claim_text: All 14 configurations meet the planner's window-mean targets (TTFT/ITL under 500/50 ms) but violate the tail SLA (TTFT p99 up to 3,495 ms; burst windows also fail ITL p99).

anchor: Variants A and B fail alike, so loop tuning is not the issue.
claim_text: Both variants A and B fail similarly, indicating loop tuning is not the issue.

anchor: The defect is the mean-based capacity conversion: sizing replicas so mean throughput meets mean demand leaves no room for the tail the SLA prices.
claim_text: The defect is mean-based capacity conversion: sizing replicas to meet mean demand leaves no capacity for the tail that the SLA prices.

anchor: Holding a 60-second replica lead and tightening the planner's window-mean targets from 400/40 to 200/20 ms on burst1 raises GPU-hours monotonically (18.6 → 20.4) while TTFT p99 stays pinned near 1,616 ms --- a 10% spend increase buying nothing.
claim_text: On burst1 with 60-second replica lead, tightening window-mean targets from 400/40 to 200/20 ms increases GPU-hours from 18.6 to 20.4 (10% increase) while TTFT p99 remains ~1,616 ms.

anchor: Burst1's 220-minute onset gives a trailing window ample time, yet tightening the mean targets still cannot buy the tail: the failure is the conversion, not thrift or timing
claim_text: Despite burst1's 220-minute onset providing ample time, tightening mean targets cannot meet the tail SLA; the failure is due to conversion, not thrift or timing.

anchor: the fair strawman is identically informed with the next chapter's predictive policy: the same worker-mapping law (workers = ceil(demand / ρ) at per-worker capacity rating ρ img/s, hysteresis 3 minutes, lead L), fed by the trailing window of the observed image rate --- the correct per-pool signal, observed not forecast.
claim_text: The reactive encoder strawman uses the same worker-mapping law as the predictive policy: workers = ceil(demand / ρ) with ρ=15 img/s, 3-minute hysteresis, lead L, fed by trailing window of observed image rate (observed, not forecast).

anchor: Slow ramps (burst1, the calm day) are reactive-scalable at any tested lead
claim_text: Slow ramps (burst1 and calm day) are reactive-scalable at any tested lead.

anchor: medium onsets survive only sub-minute leads (L*=45 s, below what pod-scheduled GPU workers realistically offer).
claim_text: Medium onsets survive only sub-minute leads (L*=45 s), below what pod-scheduled GPU workers realistically offer.

anchor: burst6's one-minute onset is caught at short leads (L*=45 s) because its peak (337 img/s) drains within a batch
claim_text: Burst6 (1-min onset, peak 337 img/s) is caught at short leads (L*=45 s) because its peak drains within a batch.

anchor: burst3's one-minute onset defeats the controller at every lead, including 15 s (p99 encoder delay 9.5--54 s).
claim_text: Burst3 (1-min onset) defeats the controller at every lead, including 15 s, with p99 encoder delay 9.5-54 s.

anchor: It is the same peak against a thinner request stream: watching the right signal is necessary but not sufficient, since against a fast, high-volume onset no affordable lead delivers workers before the queue does the damage.
claim_text: For the same peak, a thinner request stream (burst3) makes reactive control insufficient; no affordable lead can deliver workers before queue damage.

anchor: The static optimum is burst-shaped: deployable only as 8 encoders + TP2×2, i.e. 4×/2× calm-day overprovisioning plus a TP-shape change no replica scaler performs
claim_text: The static optimum is burst-shaped, deployable only as 8 encoders + TP2×2, which overprovisions calm day by 4× (vision) and 2× (language) and includes a TP-shape change that no replica scaler can perform.

anchor: The reactive alternative fails on both pools for one structural reason --- information arriving too late and converted through means: the fourteen language-pool configurations meet their own window-mean law while violating the tail SLA, spend cannot buy the tail back under lead, and even the correct encoder signal read reactively loses every window whose onset is faster than the lead.
claim_text: Reactive control fails on both pools: 14 language-pool configs meet window-mean law but violate tail SLA; increased spend cannot buy tail back under lead; reactive encoder control loses every window where onset is faster than lead.

anchor: At full-trace scale (1,000,000 requests), the deployable C=8 fleet passes, the calm-day C=2 fleet fails, and reactive encoder control holds the bound for 0.687× the deployable fleet's worker-time
claim_text: At full-trace scale (1M requests), deployable C=8 fleet passes SLA, calm-day C=2 fleet fails, and reactive encoder control uses 0.687× the deployable fleet's worker-time.
